questions.question:
**Direction: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

**__Our teachers has planned of going for a picnic__ **to the Doon Valley.

options.text: Our teachers has planned a picnic
Our teachers has plan a picnic
Our teachers is planned a picnic
Our teachers have planned a picnic

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **"Our teachers have planned a picnic."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the part, **"**Our teachers has planned of going for a picnic__**."**
 
• The subject **"teachers"** is plural, so the correct verb form is **"have planned."**
 
• The sentence is in the present perfect tense, indicating that the planning has already taken place.
 
• So, there is no need to use **"of going for a picnic."**
 
• The correct answer is option 4.

 

**Correct sentence**: *__**Our teachers have planned a picnic**__ to the Doon Valley.*

questions.question:
**Directions: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No improvement’.**

__As many as__ I care for her, I still have to disagree with her on this topic.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'As much as'**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• In the underlined segment, the **adjective 'many'** is **incorrect**.
 
• The **adjective 'many'** means **a large number**. We use "**as many as**" for **countable nouns**.
 
• The **adjective 'much'** means **a great amount or quantity**. We use "**as much as**" for **uncountable nouns**.
 
• Therefore, the **adjective 'much'** should be used **in place of** the **adjective 'many'**.

 

Hence, the correct answer is **option 1**.

**The Correct Sentence is:** ***As much as** I care for her, I still have to disagree with her on this topic*.

questions.question:
**Direction: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.**

Neither John nor Simon **__are coming to the meeting__**.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **"is coming to the meeting."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The subject of the sentence is **"Neither John nor Simon"**, which is a compound subject.
 
• When **"neither ...... nor"** links singular terms, the verb is singular.
 
• When the subjects are connected by **"nor",** the verb should agree with the subject closest to it.
 
 
• **Example: ***Neither the car nor the truck is available.*
 
 
 
• In this case, it is **"Simon."**
 
• **"Is coming" **is the correct verb form for the singular subject **"Simon".**
 
• The correct answer is Option 4.

 

**Correct sentence:** *Neither John nor Simon **is coming to the meeting**__.*

questions.question:
**Direction: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.**

The playground was way **__large then I had__** imagined, and in cleaning it, my back began to ache.
questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is "larger than I had."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When two items/people/situations are compared, a comparative degree is used by putting ‘er’ to the adjective word or "more" with the adjective in association with the word ‘than’.

 
 
• Example: 
 
• *She is more cheerful than her sister.*
 
• *She is smarter than her sister.*​
 
 
 
• Here, we need the comparative degree of the word 'large.'
 
• The comparative degree of 'large' is formed by adding "er" after the positive degree of the adjective "large."
 
• Therefore, the comparative degree of "large" is "larger."
 
• Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Correct sentence__: *The playground was way __**larger than I had**__ imagined, and in cleaning it, my back began to ache.*

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

Every nook and corner __of the house were unclean.__
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **of the house was unclean **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the subject-verb agreement.
 
• The basic rule states that a singular subject takes a singular verb while a plural subject takes a plural verb.
 
• Replace '**were**' with '**was**' to correct the sentence.
 
• When two or more singular nouns joined by ‘**AND**’ are preceded by ‘**EACH**’ and ‘**EVERY**’ the pronoun must be singular.
 
 
• **For example-** *Every student and every teacher took his or her seat.*
 
 
 
• So, '**was**' should be used here.
 
• The meaning of "**every nook and corner**" is every place: everywhere: every part of the house.

Hence, the correct answer is **option 4**.

**Corrected sentence: ***Every nook and corner of the house was unclean.__*

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the highlighted word(s) in the given sentence.

The fleets of Anthony were __not merely defeated, also destroyed__ by Augustus Caesar.

options.text: not only defeated, but also destroyed

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. not only defeated, but also destroyed .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence uses the phrase “not merely defeated, also destroyed.” This is grammatically incorrect and does not convey the intended meaning effectively.
 
• The phrase "not only... but also" is the correct correlative conjunction pair that expresses both actions (defeated and destroyed) effectively.
 
• By choosing **option 1**, the sentence becomes grammatically correct and clear in meaning.

Correct sentence: *The fleets of Anthony were not only defeated, but also destroyed by Augustus Caesar*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Use of Correlative Conjunctions:**
 
 
• **Not only... but also:** Used to join two related ideas, emphasizing both parts equally.
 
• **Example:** She is not only intelligent, but also hardworking.
 
• It ensures proper parallelism in sentence structure.
 
 
 
• **Common Errors to Avoid:**
 
 
• Incorrect pairing of correlative conjunctions, such as "not merely... also." This disrupts the flow and correctness of the sentence.
 
• Ensure that the phrases following "not only" and "but also" are grammatically similar for proper parallelism.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

Not only is my brother intelligent __though hard working__ too.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **but hard working**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Replace the conjunction "**though**" with "**but**" to correct the sentence.
 
• “**But**” indicates a complete negation and is usually used after a comma, in the middle of a sentence.
 
 
• **For example- ***The food wasn't good, but at least it was cheap.*
 
 
 
• “**Though**” is usually used at the end of a sentence and indicates a partial negation.
 
 
• **For example- ***She seemed healthy, though she is thin.*
 
 
 
• **​**We use "**though**" to introduce a subordinate clause in which you mention something that contrasts with what you are saying in the main clause.
 
• "**But**" is used to add emphasis to a sentence.
 
• The implied meaning of the given sentence is: My sibling is not only smart but also diligent.
 
• Some two-part subjects are joined by “either...or,” “neither...nor,” or “not only...but also.” In these cases, the verb should agree with the subject closest to the verb.
 
• In this sentence, "**not only**" is already mentioned. So, we should use "**but**" according to the subject-verb agreement rule.

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 2** which can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

**Corrected sentence:** *Not only is my brother intelligent but __hard working too.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• Let us look at the use of the other words given in the options.
 
 
• **Or**: Or is a conjunction that connects two or more possibilities or alternatives. It connects words, phrases and clauses which are the same grammatical type.

 
 
• **For example-** *Which do you prefer? Leather or suede?*
 
 
 
• **So**: It is used as a subordinating conjunction to introduce clauses of result or decision.
 
 
• For example- *You are right, of course, so I think we will accept what the bank offers.*
 
 
 
• **Yet**: It is used as an adverb to refer to a time which starts in the past and continues up to the present. We use it mostly in negative statements or questions in the present perfect.
 
 
• For example- *Kevin hasn't registered for class yet.*

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

He __was sitting besides his__ best friend during the event.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'was sitting beside his'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is grammatically incorrect.
 
• Here, **'was sitting beside his'** should be used instead of **'was sitting besides his'.**
 
• The word "**besides**" means "**in addition to**" or "**apart from**," while "**beside**" means "**next to**" or **"by the side of."** Therefore, in this sentence, "**beside**" is the correct word to use because it describes the **physical position** of the person sitting next to their friend.
 
• Additionally, the sentence is grammatically correct because it has a **subject** ("**he**"), a **verb** ("**was sitting**"), and an **object** ("**his best friend**"). The **preposition** "**beside**" correctly shows the relationship between the **subject** and the **object** in the sentence.
 
• Finally, the phrase* "during the event" *provides additional information about the setting of the action, which adds context to the sentence.
 
• Thus, the correct answer is **Option 2.**

 

**Correct Sentence:__** *He __**was sitting beside his**__ best friend during the event.*

questions.question:
In the following sentence the underlined part contains as error. Alternatives to the underlined part are given as options. Select the correct alternative.

Ahuja is a __cleverest__ lawyer.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the use of the superlative form "**cleverest**" with the article "**a**".
 
• Superlative adjectives are used with the definite article "**the**."
 
• Using "**a cleverest**" is grammatically incorrect because it mixes an indefinite article with a superlative adjective.
 
• Since no comparison is being made among all lawyers, the correct form should simply be "**a clever lawyer**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1: clever**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Ahuja is a clever lawyer."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Comparative degree** (e.g., cleverer/more clever) is used when comparing two entities.
 
• **Superlative degree** (e.g., cleverest/most clever) is used when comparing more than two entities and should be preceded by "**the**".
 
• When no comparison is involved, the **positive degree** ("clever") is used with the indefinite article "a."

questions.question:
In the following sentence the underlined part contains an error. Alternatives to the underlined part are given as options. Select the correct alternative.

When they left for Mexico, their house was in __good__ condition than it is now.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '4' i.e. better .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence compares the condition of the house in two different time periods — when they left for Mexico and its current state.
 
• In such comparisons, the correct word to use is the comparative form of "good," which is **"better."**
 
• Using other options like "more good," "excellent," or "best" is grammatically incorrect or contextually inappropriate in this case.

Correct sentence: *When they left for Mexico, their house was in **better** condition than it is now*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Comparative adjectives:**

 
 
• Used to compare two things, e.g., "better," "worse," "taller," etc.
 
• Formed by adding "-er" to short adjectives or by using "more" with longer adjectives.
 
• **Example:** This book is **better** than that one.
 
 
 
• **Superlative adjectives:**

 
 
• Used to show the highest degree of comparison among three or more things, e.g., "best," "worst," "tallest," etc.
 
• Formed by adding "-est" to short adjectives or by using "most" with longer adjectives.
 
• **Example:** This is the **best** book in the library.

questions.question:
**Directions: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select ‘No substitution’.**

Many of the apples __was rotten__.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'were rotten.'​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the underlined part of the sentence, the singular form of the verb 'was' is incorrect.
 
• The subject of the sentence is composed of the plural noun 'apples'.
 
• We know that a plural subject always takes a plural verb.
 
• Therefore, the plural form of the verb 'were' should be used in place of the singular form 'was'.

 

Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

Correct sentence: *Many of the apples **were rotten***.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• Subjects and verbs must agree with one another in number (singular or plural).
 
• Thus, if a subject is singular, its verb must also be singular; if a subject is a plural, its verb must also be plural.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/51867102c7c2f369f6e29d2efe025e3b3367c68261ec20262828d84ca5c8f854.png] **Hinglish__**

 
• वाक्य के रेखांकित भाग में '**was**' क्रिया का **एकवचन रूप गलत है**।
 
• वाक्य का subject, **बहुवचन संज्ञा** 'apples' से बना है।
 
• हम जानते हैं कि बहुवचन **subject** हमेशा बहुवचन क्रिया लेता है ।
 
• इसलिए, क्रिया का बहुवचन रूप '**were**' एकवचन रूप 'was' के स्थान पर प्रयोग किया जाना चाहिए।

 

अत: सही उत्तर विकल्प 1 है ।

सही वाक्य: *Many of the apples were rotten*.

Priya has been working in this school __from June 2017__.

__
 
• The present perfect continuous is a verb tense that shows an action or state that either occurred at an indefinite time in the past or began in the past and continued to the present time.
 
• The structure is given below:
 
 
• Subject + has/have + been + V1 + -ing + since/for + object.
 
 
 
• Since is used for a point of time (1982, last month, etc.) whereas for is used for any duration (4 days, 6 months, etc.).
 
• Example:
 
 
• *​The factory has been working well since 1945.*
 
 
 
• As a point of time i.e. 1917 has been given in the question, 'since' will replace 'from' in the underlined part.
 
• In this way, we are left with the only correct choice as the 4th option.

 

Correct Sentence__: *Priya has been working in this school **since June 2017.***

questions.question:

He not only got a scholarship and also a good job.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**and also**".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the conjunction '**and**' used is **incorrect**. We know with "not only", we use "but also" in a sentence.
 
• "**Not only**" and "**but also**" are correlative conjunctions work in pairs to join words, phrases, or clauses.
 
• The construction "**not only....but also**" is called **correlative conjunction**. It is **used to present two related pieces of information**.
 
• **Both pieces of information** are being presented by the writer as **surprising or unexpected**, with the **second one being even more surprising than the first**.
 
• The **first piece of information** comes **after** **not only**, and the **second piece of information** comes **after but also**.
 
• **Hence**, the correct answer is **option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence__: ***He not only got a scholarship **but also** a good job.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Correlative conjunctions** work in pairs to join words, phrases, or clauses. The correlative conjunctions are **either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or.**

The correct answer is **Option 3.**

A conjunction phrase 'as soon as' is used here to indicate an action that happens immediately.

Thus the correct sentence will be: *The students stood up __as soon as__ the Principal entered the class.*
